newsitem.title: USA: Georgia opens music museum in home of southern rock.
newsitem.headline: Georgia opens music museum in home of southern rock.

text.p: The city where Little Richard was born, Otis Redding grew up, James Brown got his start and the Allman Brothers pioneered southern rock celebrated its rich musical heritage Sunday by opening a $6.5 million Georgia Music Hall of Fame.

The 43,000-square-foot, three-story museum, which recreates a music festival in a small Georgia village, features more than 150 artists, including blues pioneer "Ma" Rainey, the Allman Brothers, and groups like R.E.M. and the B-52's.

The music museum, funded with state and private money, has been a pet project of Governor Zell Miller for almost 20 years. Miller is giving the museum proceeds from the sale of his newly-updated book about Georgia musicians called "They Heard Georgia Singing."

"The mother of the blues, Gertrude 'Ma' Rainey, was from Columbus, Georgia," Miller said. "The father of gospel music, Thomas Dorsey, is from Villa Rica, Georgia. Johnny Mercer, one of the great lyricists of all times, is from Savannah."
James Brown got his start in Macon, backed by a local car dealer. Richard Penniman, better known as Little Richard, wrote "Tutti Frutti" while washing dishes at the Greyhound bus station in Macon.

"I am the architect of rock and roll. I am the originator. I am the emancipator. I am the man who started it all," the ebullient Richard said at the gala opening of the museum on Saturday night. The Hall of Fame opened to the general public on Sunday.
Macon was also home of the Capricorn Records label, which launched the Allman Brothers Band, the Marshall Tucker Band, Johnny Jenkins and Wet Willie in the 1970s.

Governor Miller said his interest in music was sparked by watching fiddlers in the north Georgia mountains. "Every time there was something in a magazine or something in the newspaper, I'd tear it out and put it in a box," he said.
"We've heard that story before, but we haven't seen the box," said assistant curator Deborah Besser, who stressed the museum's collection is in its early stages.

While visitors can listen to a two-hour radio programme on Georgia musicians in one of the museum's small, themed rooms, most of the Hall of Fame is dedicated to displays of memorabilia, with little history or background.

Among the items on display are the shoes singer-songwriter Otis Redding was wearing when he died in a plane crash in 1967, a dollhouse from the collection of country singer Brenda Lee, and the tape machine James Brown used to record his first hit, "Please, Please, Please."
A gift shop selling Georgia music includes recordings by Jimi Hendrix, because the guitarist spent two years in Atlanta. There is also a museum display dedicated to southern rock band Lynyrd Skynyrd.
"They're from Florida, but Georgia claims them too," said Judy Van Zant, who lent items to the museum including musical instruments, stage costumes, and an opened bottle of Jack Daniels whiskey.
The museum also highlights country, jazz and swing music and the white and black gospel music unique to the South.
Organisers, who had hoped to open the museum before the Summer Olympics in Atlanta, estimate the Hall of Fame will attract 175,000 to 250,000 people annually.
